'''Daniel Thomas Ksepka''' (born March 1, 1980) is an American [[paleontologist]]. His research focuses on the evolution of birds and reptiles, being specialized in [[penguins]].

== Biography ==
Ksepka received a Bachelor of Science degree from [[Rutgers University]] in 2002 and a Master of Science degree from [[Columbia University]] in 2005. He spent five years at the [[American Museum of Natural History]] in [[New York City]], gaining extensive experience in the conservation and study of natural history specimens such as fossils, skeletal material, skins, and geological samples. In 2007, under the supervision of [[Mark Norell]], he earned his Ph.D. at Columbia University with a dissertation entitled ''Phylogeny, histology and functional morphology of fossil penguins (Sphenisciformes)''.<ref name=bio1>{{cite web |title=Daniel T. Ksepka |url=https://www.americanscientist.org/author/daniel_t._ksepka |website=American Scientist |access-date=19 September 2025}}</ref>

From 2009 to 2013, he was an assistant professor at [[North Carolina State University]], and from 2009 to 2014 he was a research associate at the [[North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences]]. In 2011, he became a research associate at the [[Smithsonian Institution]], and in 2012, a research associate at the [[Field Museum of Natural History]] in [[Chicago]]. From January 2013 to May 2014, he completed his postdoctoral phase at the [[National Evolutionary Synthesis Center]] in [[Durham, North Carolina]]. Since June 2014, he has been curator at the [[Bruce Museum]] in [[Greenwich, Connecticut]].<ref name=bio2>{{cite web |title=Daniel Ksepka–Penguins, Past and Present |url=https://nuttallclub.org/meetings/daniel-ksepka-penguins-past-and-present/ |website=Nutall Ornithological Club |access-date=19 September 2025}}</ref>

Ksepka has curated numerous exhibitions at the Bruce Museum including Monsters and Mermaids: Unraveling Natural History’s Greatest Hoaxes,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ksepka |first=Daniel T. |title=5 of the Greatest Natural History Hoaxes of All Time |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/5-of-the-greatest-natural-history-hoaxes-of-all-time/ |access-date=2025-09-28 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> Conservation Through the Arts: Celebrating the Federal Duck Stamp,<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-10-22 |title=Ducks Do More Than You Might Think to Help Save the Planet |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/22/arts/duck-stamp-bruce-museum.html |access-date=2025-09-28 |language=en}}</ref> and On Thin Ice: Alaska’s Warming Wilderness.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-04-25 |title=A Visit to Alaska Inspires a Climate Change Exhibit in Connecticut |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/25/arts/design/bruce-museum-alaska-climate-change.html |access-date=2025-09-28 |language=en}}</ref>

His research focuses on bird evolution, especially [[phylogeny]], [[molecular clock|divergence dating]], and the evolution of wing-propelled diving in penguins. In 2014, he described ''[[Pelagornis sandersi]]'', the largest known flying bird, in a study that focused particularly on flight pattern modeling.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ksepka |first=Daniel T. |date=2014-07-22 |title=Flight performance of the largest volant bird |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1320297111 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=111 |issue=29 |pages=10624–10629 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1320297111 |pmc=4115518 |pmid=25002475}}</ref> He also studies the reconstruction of brain size evolution in [[dinosaurs]] and [[birds]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ksepka |first=Daniel T. |last2=Balanoff |first2=Amy M. |last3=Smith |first3=N. Adam |last4=Bever |first4=Gabriel S. |last5=Bhullar |first5=Bhart-Anjan S. |last6=Bourdon |first6=Estelle |last7=Braun |first7=Edward L. |last8=Burleigh |first8=J. Gordon |last9=Clarke |first9=Julia A. |last10=Colbert |first10=Matthew W. |last11=Corfield |first11=Jeremy R. |last12=Degrange |first12=Federico J. |last13=De Pietri |first13=Vanesa L. |last14=Early |first14=Catherine M. |last15=Field |first15=Daniel J. |date=2020-06-08 |title=Tempo and Pattern of Avian Brain Size Evolution |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982220304309 |journal=Current Biology |volume=30 |issue=11 |pages=2026–2036.e3 |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2020.03.060 |issn=0960-9822|hdl=11370/b9b6c014-6b19-4ae6-b3d0-6e76c199a07e |hdl-access=free }}</ref> In 2017, he co-described ''[[Tsidiiyazhi abini]]'', the oldest known tree-dwelling bird species from the [[Neornithes]], which lived about 62.5 million years ago during the [[Paleocene]].<ref name=bio1 /><ref name=bio2 /><ref>{{cite web |title=Stories by Daniel T. Ksepka  |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/author/daniel-t-ksepka/ |website=Scientif American |access-date=19 September 2025}}</ref>
